strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it provides a systematic preliminary analysis (Section 3) of where redundancy arises in the LVLM pipeline and identifies two orthogonal redundancy factors (intra-modal diversity and cross-modal task relevance) that prior attention-based criteria overlook. The empirical observations (attention positional bias, 'information migration' across decoder layers) are clearly presented and support the design.

The proposed ToDRE method is simple, training-free, plug-and-play, and well-specified: greedy k-center selection with a principled pivot initialization (with distinct handling of AnyRes images and video), plus an adaptive layer-selection rule for dropping all visual tokens based on measurable cross-modal attention ratios (Eq. 7).

Experimental evidence is extensive and convincing: 8 image + 4 video benchmarks, two model scales (7B/13B), consistent outperformance of strong recent training-free baselines (FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2) at both 25% and 10% retain ratios, and notably at extreme 90% compression ToDRE retains 95.1% of performance while other methods drop to 86-92%.

Efficiency and ablation studies are thorough: Table 3 reports FLOPs/memory/throughput trade-offs; Table 4 disentangles the contributions of Stage 1 vs. Stage 2; Appendix C.1/C.2 ablate the threshold and candidate layers, and Appendix D validates the decoding-stage attention assumption with extra visualizations.
Compatibility with efficient attention operators, generalization across image and video modalities, and a candid limitations section add practical value and transparency.
weaknesses: Backbone diversity is limited: all main results use LLaVA-NeXT with Vicuna (7B/13B). Given the method's training-free, architecture-agnostic claim, evaluation on at least one modern backbone (e.g., Qwen2-VL, InternVL, LLaVA-OneVision) would substantially strengthen generalization claims; transferability remains unverified.

Baseline exclusions weaken fair comparison: FastV and SparseVLM are dropped from the 13B table, and SparseVLM/GlobalCom2 from video experiments, justified only by 'transferability issues'. Reported failure details or tuned configurations for these baselines would make the comparisons more convincing.

Efficiency claims are somewhat inconsistent across the paper: the abstract advertises a 2.6x speed-up (derived from Table 4 total-time reductions), while Table 3 reports 1.9x throughput on POPE. The discrepancy across metrics/settings should be stated more carefully; also it is unclear whether the timing numbers include the O(n^2) pairwise-similarity overhead of the k-center step and attention-ratio monitoring, which the limitation section acknowledges but does not quantify.

The theoretical appendix (Appendix B) is weak and arguably vacuous: it assumes vision and text embeddings lie in mutually orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), which does not hold in any actual LVLM, and then 'proves' statistical independence of the two redundancy measures from that assumption. This provides little genuine support for the two-stage paradigm and risks overclaiming; presenting it as an empirical observation instead would be more honest.

The 'information migration' observation and stage-2 full visual token removal build closely on prior work (VTW [35]); the novelty lies mainly in the forward-pass layer-selection metric and combination with diversity selection, which is incremental though effectively engineered.

Some design choices appear tuned to the evaluated setup (e.g., tau = 0.03, layer set L/2, 5L/8, 6L/8, 7L/8, k = 10%), and sensitivity across model families/larger k ranges is only partially explored. Minor issues include typos and the redundant duplicated numbers in the Table 4 text (30:38 repeated for both ratios).

strengths: The paper is well-motivated and clearly written; the two proposed factors (token diversity and token-task relevance) are analyzed in a structured way, and the 'information migration' observation during prefilling is a useful empirical contribution.

The empirical evaluation is broad: twelve image- and video-language benchmarks, two model scales (7B/13B), efficiency measurements (FLOPs, memory, throughput), and multiple ablations (threshold τ, layer selection, stage contributions), which is more thorough than many competing token-pruning papers.
The method is training-free and plug-and-play, and reported results (95.1% average retained performance at 90% pruning) are competitive with or better than the baselines evaluated.

Reproducibility is aided by detailed benchmark descriptions (Appendix A), pseudocode for the k-center selection (Algorithm 1), and qualitative visualizations; limitations are honestly discussed (Appendix F).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: both core components are largely recombinations of existing ideas. Diversity-based visual token selection was already proposed in DivPrune [2] (cited in related work but conspicuously NOT included as an empirical baseline — this is a critical omission since it is essentially the same Stage 1 idea), and dropping visual tokens in later LLM layers builds directly on VTW [35]'s information-migration finding, with only a different layer-selection heuristic. The claimed novelty of 'rethinking the criterion of redundancy' is therefore overstated.

The theoretical analysis in Appendix B is weak and effectively circular: it assumes visual and textual tokens occupy mutually orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), an assumption that is manifestly false in actual LVLMs where modalities share one embedding space and cross-modal attention is central (which the paper itself demonstrates in Figure 2). Proving independence of the two redundancy measures under a contrived orthogonality assumption does not validate the two-stage design on real models and should not be presented as a 'theoretical proof validating the rationale'.

Backbone coverage is narrow: all experiments use LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B only. Given that the paper criticizes FastV/SparseVLM for poor transferability across backbones, evaluating only a single LVLM family is a significant weakness; results on Qwen2-VL/2.5-VL or InternVL would be needed to support the generalization claim.

Weakened baseline comparisons: FastV and SparseVLM are dropped from the 13B table and SparseVLM/GlobalCom2 from the video table, citing 'transferability issues' without reporting the numbers; comparisons would be more convincing with failures shown explicitly.

Inconsistent headline claims: the abstract and conclusion claim a '2.6× speed-up', but Table 3 reports a 1.9× throughput improvement over the baseline on POPE, and the marginal Stage 2 gains (≈0.3–0.4% performance, ~1–2 min time reduction) suggest the second stage contributes little beyond Stage 1, contrary to the framing that both stages are equally essential.

The computational overhead of the greedy k-center selection (O(nk) similarity computations over ~2880 tokens per sample) is acknowledged in the limitations but never quantified in the main experiments; a latency breakdown of selection cost vs. savings is missing.

Several small inconsistencies undermine polish: the Section 5.3 text cites 'from 30:38 to 29:51' at the 25% ratio while Table 4 reports 44:40 to 43:09, and the decoding-stage claims rely on qualitative attention plots from only 100 samples per benchmark.

strengths: The paper identifies and empirically motivates two complementary redundancy factors (intra-modal diversity and cross-modal task relevance) with clear preliminary analyses (Figures 1, 2, 5) that directly motivate the two-stage design.

Comprehensive evaluation: 12 image/video benchmarks across two model scales, with strong results at extreme compression (95.1% of baseline performance at 10% retention), including cases where pruning surpasses the uncompressed baseline on video tasks.

The two-stage framework is training-free, plug-and-play, and compatible with efficient attention operators; the ablation studies (Tables 4-6) carefully isolate the contribution of each stage, the threshold τ, and the layer-selection strategy.

Efficiency is measured end-to-end (FLOPs, peak memory, throughput, wall-clock time) rather than only FLOPs, and the discussion of where gains arise (prefilling vs. decoding) is honest about limitations on short-output benchmarks.

The method generalizes to video and to 13B models without retuning, in contrast to some baselines that degrade under transfer; the appendix provides detailed reproduction information (benchmarks, sample counts, hardware).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental and the framing slightly overstates originality. Diversity-based visual token selection via greedy farthest-point/k-center sampling already exists (e.g., DivPrune [2], which the paper cites as related work but does not compare against experimentally), and attention-ratio-based layer selection is closely related to VTW [35]. The main novelty is the combination; a direct comparison with DivPrune under identical settings is needed to substantiate the claim that these factors were 'largely neglected'.

The theoretical appendix (Section B) is weak and does not support the empirical claims: it assumes visual and text embeddings occupy mutually orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0), which is plainly unrealistic for a shared projector embedding space, and the resulting covariance-independence result is essentially tautological under the assumed orthogonality. It adds little validation of the two-stage paradigm.

There is an inconsistency between the abstract/conclusion (2.6× speed-up, 95.1% performance) and Table 3 (1.9× throughput speed-up on POPE, 95.1% performance), and Table 4's narrative contains errors (e.g., 'time reduced from 30:38 to 29:51' should refer to 44:40 → 43:09). Also, Table 4 reports ToDRE average of 95.5% while Table 1 reports 95.1% for the same configuration—these discrepancies need correction and explanation.

Backbone coverage is narrow: all experiments use LLaVA-NeXT (7B/13B). Given the paper's claim of architecture-agnostic robustness, results on at least one other LVLM family (e.g., LLaVA-OneVision, Qwen2-VL) would substantially strengthen the generalization claim, particularly since the pivot-selection logic is tied to AnyRes-style tiling.

Excluding baselines from the 13B and video comparisons (FastV, SparseVLM, GlobalCom2) is justified by transferability issues, but it weakens direct comparability of the headline claims; the second-best margins on those settings are therefore established against a reduced field.

The Stage 2 layer-selection design involves several heuristic choices (candidate layers L/2..7L/8, threshold τ=0.03, both ratios below threshold) whose optimality appears empirical; a sensitivity analysis across a broader range of tasks/models would improve confidence in robustness.

strengths: The paper provides a clear and well-motivated decomposition of visual token redundancy into intra-modal (diversity) and cross-modal (task relevance) components, supported by empirical analysis (FLOPs breakdown, information-migration plots across layers) rather than assertions.

Extensive empirical validation: four LVLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B), twelve image and video benchmarks, comparisons against five representative training-free baselines, plus efficiency measurements (FLOPs, memory, throughput) and ablations on pivot selection, threshold, layer choice, and stage contributions.

The method is training-free and plug-and-play, achieving strong accuracy-efficiency trade-offs (95.0% performance at 90% token pruning, 1.9-2.6x speedup), and outperforms strong diversity-based baselines like DivPrune at equal budgets.

The paper is transparent about marginal gains in some settings (e.g., decoding-stage savings are small for short-output benchmarks) and includes limitations-oriented discussion of where benefits accrue (long-form generation).
Supplementary material provides pseudocode, an ablation on candidate pruning layers and thresholds, qualitative visualizations, and case studies, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Stage 1 is essentially DivPrune's greedy diversity-based selection (the greedy max-sum diversification is borrowed from [22], and DivPrune is directly compared); Stage 2 builds directly on VTW's information-migration idea [35], replacing KL-divergence-based layer selection with a simpler attention-ratio criterion. The main contribution is the combination and the empirical demonstration that the two criteria are complementary, which is incremental.

The 'proof of orthogonality' in the supplementary is largely circular: orthogonality of the visual and text subspaces is imposed by assumption (W_V^T W_T = 0), and the Lemma then trivially follows from this assumption. It does not establish that real LVLM embeddings satisfy this property, so its theoretical value is questionable and should not be cited as 'proving' the two-stage design.

The aggregate gains from Stage 2 over Stage 1 alone are small (+0.1-0.2% accuracy, ~4% total-time reduction), raising questions about whether the added complexity and analysis justify a second stage; a more careful cost-benefit or a stronger Stage 2 variant would strengthen the case.

Some baseline exclusions are potentially unfair: FastV and SparseVLM are omitted from the 13B and video comparisons because they 'degrade when directly transferred', yet their hyperparameters could arguably have been tuned per-model; this asymmetry favors ToDRE in the average scores.

Evaluation is confined to ≤13B open models and mostly short-answer benchmarks; generalization to larger models, long-form generation workloads (where the claimed decoding-stage benefits should be largest), and high-resolution/document tasks is asserted rather than measured.

Practical details affecting reproducibility (e.g., exact implementation of attention-ratio computation with FlashAttention, per-sample runtime of the greedy selection at n~3000 tokens, variance over seeds for the random-pivot ablation) are underspecified in the main paper.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four LVLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B) across twelve image and video benchmarks, with consistent (if modest) improvements over the strongest baselines at both 25% and 10% retention ratios.

The two-stage decomposition of redundancy into intra-modal (diversity) and cross-modal (task relevance) factors is a reasonable and clearly articulated framing, supported by ablations (Table 5) showing each stage contributes and that they compose well.

The relevance-driven stage is a practical forward-pass criterion (cross-modal attention ratios at depth 7L/8) replacing VTW's calibration-set-dependent KL divergence, which is a genuine usability improvement for a training-free, plug-and-play method.

Thorough supplementary material: pivot-strategy, threshold, and layer-selection ablations, decoding-stage attention analysis, pseudocode, and qualitative comparisons improve reproducibility and transparency.
The paper is generally well-written and organized, with clear motivation via the FLOPs decomposition and the 'information migration' observation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over prior work. Stage 1 (greedy max-sum diversification with a pivot token) is essentially the method of DivPrune [2], which is cited and compared; the paper's own ablation (Supp. Table 1) shows a random pivot performs nearly identically, further reducing the difference to DivPrune. Stage 2 builds directly on VTW's 'information migration' observation [35]. The net contribution is a combination of two known ideas, and the measured advantage over DivPrune is small (e.g., 98.2% vs 96.6% and 95.0% vs 93.5% average; throughput 2.9 vs 2.8 samples/s).

The claimed theoretical contribution is weak and arguably circular. The appendix 'proves' orthogonality/independence of intra- and cross-modal redundancy by *assuming* orthogonal subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0) by construction; the conclusion then follows trivially. Real vision-language embeddings are not orthogonal in this sense, and the lemma provides no support for the actual design choices (greedy max-sum selection, threshold τ, layer 7L/8). Presenting this as a proof that the two-stage paradigm is 'validated' overstates the result considerably.

Efficiency claims are somewhat inconsistent and underwhelming relative to the abstract: '2.6× speed-up' appears while Table 4 reports 1.9× throughput on POPE, and short-output benchmarks (the majority evaluated) yield modest gains—the paper itself concedes decoding-stage savings are marginal in practice. FLOPs reduction (~81%) is not matched by wall-clock improvements.

Baselines are selectively excluded: FastV and SparseVLM are dropped from the 13B and video comparisons citing transferability, while ToDRE's transferability is presented as a strength. This asymmetry weakens the comparative evidence at larger scales and on video.

Retention of only 288 tokens via pure diversity selection raises robustness concerns not systematically studied: diversity-based selection is question-agnostic, so behavior on fine-grained/localization tasks or high-resolution OCR-heavy inputs (beyond the single motivating example in Figure 1) deserves more analysis. Gains on some video benchmarks come with regressions on others (e.g., MLVU drops at 10%).

The contribution type is best characterized as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General: the algorithmic core is inherited, and the value lies in the engineered two-stage pipeline and empirical study. Under that lens the empirical evidence is adequate but the system-level novelty is thin, and the paper does not discuss limitations or failure cases.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis: the 'information migration' observation (Figure 2) and the decomposition of redundancy into intra-modal (diversity) and cross-modal (task relevance) components give the two-stage design a principled rationale rather than being an ad-hoc heuristic.

Simple, training-free, and plug-and-play method: the greedy max-sum diversification plus threshold-based layer pruning requires no retraining and is compatible with FlashAttention, making it easy to adopt.

Comprehensive empirical validation: four LVLM backbones (LLaVA-NeXT-7B/13B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2-8B), twelve image and video benchmarks, multiple retention ratios (25%/10%), and consistent superiority over strong recent baselines (FastV, SparseVLM, FasterVLM, GlobalCom2, DivPrune), including cases where pruning slightly outperforms the unpruned baseline.

Efficiency results are concrete and honest: 2.6x speed-up, ~14.5% memory reduction, and an ablation (Table 5) that cleanly separates the contributions of each stage, including the candid acknowledgment that Stage 2's decoding-stage gains are marginal for short-answer tasks.

Thorough appendix: pseudocode, pivot-selection, threshold, and layer-selection ablations, decoding-stage attention analysis, and qualitative case studies support reproducibility and the design choices.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty of Stage 1: greedy max-sum diversification with cosine similarity closely resembles DivPrune's diversity-based greedy selection [2]; the main distinctions (pivot selection, embedding-space operation, video pivot handling) are incremental. The headline advantage over DivPrune in throughput is only 0.1 samples/s, so the practical contribution of the added Stage 2 should be weighed carefully.

The claimed 'proof' of orthogonality between intra- and cross-modal redundancy (Appendix Sec. 2) is weak: the orthogonality of visual and text subspaces (W_V^T W_T = 0) is assumed by construction rather than derived from or verified against actual LVLM embeddings, so the zero-covariance conclusion is essentially an artifact of the assumption. The contribution bullet 'we prove that inter-token diversity and token-task relevance are two orthogonal factors' overstates what is shown.

Stage 2's benefit is small in the reported settings: because most benchmarks require short answers, decoding-stage savings are limited, and the layer/threshold mechanism adds hyperparameters (tau, candidate layers at 7L/8) tuned empirically. The generality of the efficiency gains to long-generation workloads is asserted but not experimentally demonstrated.

Some comparisons weaken fairness: FastV and SparseVLM are excluded from the 13B and video evaluations citing transferability issues, while ToDRE's own hyperparameters were also selected on 7B models; a like-for-like discussion would strengthen the claims. The performance gains on video (Table 2) over DivPrune are within roughly 0.2-0.6%, which is close to evaluation noise.

No discussion of limitations or societal impact; also, greedy selection over ~3000 tokens involves O(nk) similarity computations per image, whose overhead relative to the overall pipeline is not quantified.
